text:
Diversity and Evolution of Life
THE KINGDOMS MONERA, PROTOCTISTA AND FUNGI
The Kingdom Monera which includes all the bacteria including blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) and the Protoctista which includes the protozoa, the diatoms and some algae are in a way the simplest among the living world. All bacteria, majority of protoctists and many fungi are microscopic and generally referred to as microorganisms. You will learn about the three kingdoms in this lesson.
summary: Explore the fundamental characteristics of the three kingdoms: Monera, Protoctista, and Fungi. Discover the simplicity and diversity of life forms, including bacteria like cyanobacteria and various microorganisms such as protozoa and fungi.

text:
The single celled bacterium has a cell wall made of the compound peptidoglycan covering the cell membrane; and a single circular (upring-like) chromosome. The cell has ribosomes but no membrane bound organelles. Let us get to know some details of these parts (Fig. 2.1).
Note the following parts of a bacterium in the figure (Fig. 2.1). The outermost covering is the cell wall.
Cell wall
All prokaryotes have a rigid cell wall, which protects and gives shape to the cell. The cell wall is made up of a chemical, peptidoglycan, unique to bacteria, lipids, polysaccharides and some proteins.
Pili (Singular: pilus)
Pili are short and thin thread like tubular structures projecting out from the cell wall in some bacteria.
Flagella
Some bacteria move with the help of one or more flagella. Flagella are longer and thicker than pili. Their structure is different from flagella of eukaryotes.
Plasma Membrane
Plasma membrane, present below the cell wall, encloses the cytoplasm and other cell contents. It is made up of lipids and proteins, as in eukaryotes.
Diversity and Evolution of Life
Genetic Material
One circular chromosome made of a double helical molecule of DNA is located in a region of the cytoplasm called nucleoid. Since the chromosome is not lodged within a true nucleus, bacteria are termed as prokaryotes. Hence Monera is the prokaryotic kingdom. Apart from the chromosome as several species of bacteria possess one or more additional rings of DNA called plasmids, which replicate along with bacterial chromosome and bear genes for antibiotic resistance and act as the sex factor or F-factor providing the property of male sex to the cell that bears the sex-factor or the F-factor.
Cell Organelles
Membrane bound organelles like endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, chloroplast, and golgi complex are absent. Only 70s ribosomes are present, which are different from those of eukaryotes (see lesson 1 and 4).
Prokaryotes have no nuclear membrane around genetic material and no membrane bound cell organelles except mesosomes. They have only the 70s ribosomes.
summary: Bacteria are single-celled organisms with a cell wall composed of peptidoglycan, protecting and shaping the cell. Inside, they have a circular chromosome located in the nucleoid region, along with ribosomes for protein synthesis, but lack membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotic cells.

summary: Nutritionally, bacteria can be classified into four categories based on their metabolic needs. Bacterial respiration involves the breakdown of food within mesosomes to release energy, similar to cellular respiration in more complex organisms. Bacteria primarily reproduce asexually through binary fission, doubling their population every 20 minutes under optimal conditions. Some bacteria also undergo a form of sexual recombination, a process distinct from that seen in higher life forms, which allows for genetic diversity and evolution.

summary: These organisms, previously known as blue-green algae, were crucial in early Earth's development. They performed photosynthesis, releasing oxygen that significantly increased atmospheric oxygen levels. Compared to bacteria, cyanobacteria have larger cells and always perform oxygenic photosynthesis, unlike some bacteria which may conduct anoxygenic photosynthesis without releasing oxygen. Additionally, while some bacteria can reproduce through conjugation, this method has also been observed in certain cyanobacteria.

1. Amoeba
Amoeba is commonly found in the mud, in freshwater ponds and ditches containing decaying leaves. (Fig. 2.5a)
Reproduction: Sexual reproduction is uncommon in Amoeba.
Asexual reproduction is by binary fission. (Fig. 2.5b)
2. Entamoeba
One common species is Entamoeba histolytica which caues amoebic dysentery in humans. It is amoeboid in form. The new host gets infected when the cyst is swallowed along with contaminated food or water. The cyst bursts and releases Entamoeba in the intestines where it causes local abscesses (open injury). The symptoms of amoebic dysentery are abdominal pain, nausea and presence of blood and mucus with stool.
3. Plasmodium (The malarial parasite)
The life cycle of Plasmodium has both asexual and sexual phases.
Male Anopheles cannot cause malaria as it feeds on plant juices and not the human blood.

Euglena is abundantly found in stagnant waters such as pools, ponds and ditches containing decaying organic matter. (Fig. 2.7)

Colour of the Red Sea is due to the dominant occurrence of a blue-green alga, Trichodesmium erythraeus
Structurally the algae have a definite cell wall, cell membrane, a nucleus, cytoplasm and choloroplast. The chloroplast is cup-shaped in Chlamydomonas and ribbon-shaped in Spirogyra. Pyrenoids, the starch containing bodies are integral part of chloroplasts in green algae.

summary: Monerans are single-celled microorganisms that have been successful due to their simple yet effective cellular structures. The protist that causes amoebiodysentery is Entamoeba histolytica, while Plasmodium is responsible for malaria. Binary fission is a common form of asexual reproduction observed in protoctists. Respiration in these organisms occurs through the mitochondria. In amoeba, contractile vacuoles play a crucial role in osmoregulation by controlling water content. Protoctists exhibit various modes of locomotion, including pseudopodia and flagella.

During warm humid days slices of bread, chapati, leather belts or shoes, develop a powdery layer on them. In lawns and flower beds, mushrooms come out. These are all fungi.
Fungi were earlier classified as plants without chlorophyll and without differentiation of their body into root, stem and leaves. They are now included, in a separate Kingdom called Fungi.
summary: Fungi grow on bread, chapati, leather, and in lawns, forming a powdery layer or mushrooms. They were once considered plant-like organisms without chlorophyll and without distinct root, stem, and leaf structures but are now recognized as a separate kingdom.

subject: Biology
chapter_title: The Kingdoms Monera, Protoctista And Fungi
text: Fungi are eukaryotic, unicellular or multicellular saprotrophs having filaments which grow through soil, wood and other substrates.
summary: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that can exist as both unicellular and multicellular forms, primarily functioning as saprotrophs. These organisms extend their filamentous structures, known as hyphae, to absorb nutrients from their surroundings, including soil, wood, and other organic materials.

The fungi are of five main kinds
1. Yeasts
Yeasts are fungi which do not produce any hyphae. These are generally in the form of single oval cells.
Fig. 2.10 shows the general structure of a yeast cell. Note the following features

Diversity and Evolution of Life
Notes

Diversity and Evolution of Life
Nutrition
Yeast is saprotrophic. It can directly absorb simple sugar (glucose) but for obtaining sucrose (cane sugar) it gives out the enzyme invertase or sucrase which breaks down sucrose into simple sugars. The simple sugars are then simply absorbed into the cell.
Yeast respires anaerobically to yield energy as follows
C_6H_{12}O_6 \longrightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2 + 2ATP
(glucose) (ethyl alcohol) (energy)
Reproduction
Yeast reproduces asexually by budding (Fig. 2.11).
Sexual reproduction may also occur by conjugation between two yeast cells. The fused contents divide by one meiosis followed by one mitosis to produce eight cells with a thick wall around each. The 8-celled structure is called ascus and each cell is called ascospore. The ascospores may be carried by wind and germinate under suitable conditions to produce new yeast cells.
2. Myxomycetes (Slime Moulds)
These consist of a naked, creeping multinucleate mass of protoplasm sometimes covering up to several square metres. The nuclei are diploid
3. Basidiomycetes (Mushrooms and Toadstools)
The vegetative part of the mycelium lies embedded in the substratum (in ground or in wood) When conditions are favourable the umbrella like mushrooms grow out with a stalk and a cap. (Fig. 2.12)
4. Lichens
These are a combination of a certain fungus and a green or blue green alga which live in a symbiotic (mutually beneficial) association: the green or blue green alga prepares food while the fungus gives protection, and absorbs water and minerals from the surroundings.

They can also break down sucrose into glucose using invertase and respire anaerobically to produce ethanol and carbon dioxide. A. Harmful Fungi
Several agricultural plants like sugarcane, maize, cereals and vegetables suffer from diseases caused by fungi.
1. Puccinia graminis (Wheat Rust)
It causes brown patches on leaf and stem of wheat plants. It decreases the yield of wheat and makes it unfit for human consumption.
2. Rhizopus or (Bread Mould) grows on bread (Fig. 2.13).
If the bread is exposed to warm and humid conditions a cottony mass develops in few days. This white cotton mass later develops a greyish black colour, because of black coloured spores.

Diversity and Evolution of Life
Diversity and Evolution of Life
Sexual reproduction (Fig. 2.14) takes place by conjugation between two neighbouring hyphae to produce a zygospore which after a period of rest undergoes meiosis followed by several mitotic cell divisions to produce a germ sporangium having a large number of haploid unicellular spores. The germ sporangium differs from asexual sporangium, as it does not have columella. When mature, the germ sporangium bursts to release spores which germinate on meeting favourable conditions and produce a new mycelium
3. In human, skin diseases like ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by fungi. Some ear infections are also caused by fungi.

summary: Harmful fungi such as Puccinia graminis cause wheat rust, leading to brown patches on wheat leaves and stems, reducing yield and making the crop unsuitable for human consumption. Rhizopus, known as bread mold, thrives in warm, humid conditions, developing a cottony white mass that later turns gray-black due to the presence of black spores. Beneficial fungi include species like Penicillium, which produce spores through complex processes involving sexual reproduction and the formation of sporangia.
